extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (or advanced undergraduates) studying algebraic geometry; readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea'
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, existence proofs, explicit constructions, and basic properties of the blow-up of a scheme along a closed subscheme; plus related topics (normal cone, exceptional divisor, behavior under regular embeddings) and an application (Hurwitz bound for automorphism groups of curves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of automorphism groups for smooth projective curves (g ≥ 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Irreducible smooth projective curves of genus g ≥ 2 have finite automorphism groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References: proof over C in [FK, 5.1], first proof in arbitrary characteristic in [Schm]. This fact is used to deduce Hurwitz's Automorphisms Theorem in characteristic 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hurwitz bound for automorphism groups (char 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: If C is an irreducible smooth projective curve over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 with genus g ≥ 2 and G is a finite group of automorphisms of C, then |G| ≤ 84(g − 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation uses the quotient curve C' = C/G, branch point data, and the Riemann–Hurwitz formula. The exercises outline constructing the morphism π : C → C' of degree |G|, noting ramification orders r_i above each branch point, and minimizing the expression (2g−2)/|G| = 2g(C')−2 + Σ (r_i−1)/r_i to get the 1/42 lower bound; equality example: g(C')=0, n=3, (r1,r2,r3)=(2,3,7). Note: in positive characteristic automorphism groups can be much larger (example cited from [Stic]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of quotient curve and branching data (exercise guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given G acting on C, let C' be the smooth projective curve corresponding to K(C)^G; there is a morphism π: C → C' of degree |G| and a faithful G-action commuting with π. Over each branch point the preimages are all ramified to the same order; if there are n branch points with ramification orders r_i, each occurs |G|/r_i times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the concrete set-up used to apply Riemann–Hurwitz; exercises (21.7.K) instruct to verify these properties and use them to compute the bound on |G|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of blow-up by universal property
rubrics_metrics.description: Bl_X Y is a Cartesian diagram EXY → Bl_X Y → Y with EXY the scheme-theoretic preimage of the center X and an effective Cartier divisor on Bl_X Y, and Bl_X Y satisfies the final-object universal property among such diagrams: any other Cartesian diagram with D an effective Cartier divisor factors uniquely through Bl_X Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology: EXY is the exceptional divisor; Bl and β denote blow-up and blow-up morphism. Uniqueness up to unique isomorphism follows by the universal property (final object). This universal-property formulation is the primary definition used to prove formal properties without computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up is unique (final object) and terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: If the blow-up exists it is unique up to unique isomorphism; the exceptional divisor EXY denotes the scheme-theoretic preimage of X and is required to be an effective Cartier divisor in the universal diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yoneda-style explanation: consider category of diagrams of the given form; blow-up is final object. Also lists alternative (archaic) names: monoidal transformation, σ-process, quadratic transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up is an isomorphism when center is empty or an effective Cartier divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is empty then Bl_X Y = Y. More generally, if X itself is an effective Cartier divisor then the blow-up is an isomorphism (identity map satisfies universal property).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation 22.2.1; useful anti-pattern to note: blowing up an effective Cartier divisor does not change the scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up is isomorphism away from the center
rubrics_metrics.description: The blow-up morphism β restricts to an isomorphism β|_{Bl_X Y − EXY}: Bl_X Y − EXY → Y − X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation 22.2.2. This justifies that blowing up only modifies the scheme along the center X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up of the whole scheme is empty
rubrics_metrics.description: If X = Y, then the blow-up Bl_X Y is the empty scheme (there is no W → Y whose pullback of X is an effective Cartier divisor unless W = ∅).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation 22.2.3; intuitive description: 'we have blown Y out of existence'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local computability of blow-ups (affine/local glueing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blow-ups can be computed locally: if U ⊂ Y is open then Bl_{X∩U} U ≅ β^{-1}(U). Also if {Y_α} is an open cover and the blow-up exists on each Y_α then it exists globally and glues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 22.2.A and 22.2.B. Practical guideline: reduce questions about blow-ups to affine/local computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of irreducibility and reducedness
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y is irreducible and X does not contain the generic point of Y, then Bl_X Y is irreducible. If Y is reduced, then Bl_X Y is reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 22.2.C. Use when deducing scheme-theoretic properties of blow-ups (e.g., blow-up of a k-variety is a k-variety; blow-up of an irreducible k-variety is irreducible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of blow-up when center is locally principal
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ Y is locally cut out by a single equation (locally principal), then the blow-up Bl_X Y exists; the construction can be reduced to affine case Spec A/(t) ⊂ Spec A and described explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 22.2.4 and Exercises 22.2.D–F provide the affine ring-theoretic construction and verifications (e.g., φ(t) not a zero-divisor, identification as scheme-theoretic closure). This is a basic nontrivial existence case and geometric interpretation as 'shaving off fuzz supported in V(t)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper transform and total transform definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed subscheme Z ⊂ Y, the scheme-theoretic preimage β^{-1}Z is called the total transform. The proper (strict) transform is the scheme-theoretic closure of β^{-1}(Z − X) inside Bl_X Y; equivalently the closure of Z ackslash X in the blow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion following definition; the Blow-up Closure Lemma formalizes that this proper transform can be computed as a blow-up on Z with center W = X∩Z when appropriate. Use these notions when computing how subvarieties change under blow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up Closure Lemma (compatibility with closed embeddings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a fibered square with closed embeddings W → Z → Y and a blow-up β: Bl_X Y → Y, form the fibered products as in (22.2.5.1)–(22.2.5.2). Let Z be the scheme-theoretic closure of (Z ×_Y Bl_X Y)  ig( W ×_Y Bl_X Y ). Then (Bl_W Z, E_{WZ}) is canonically isomorphic to (Z, E_Z); equivalently, the proper transform of Z in Bl_X Y equals the blow-up of Z along W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 22.2.7 with exercises 22.2.G and 22.2.H (tricky exercise) for proof. Practical consequence: to blow up a subscheme of Z, one can often blow up a larger ambient Y and then take the proper transform (computational tool).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proj (Rees algebra) description of the blow-up and projectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ Y is a closed subscheme cut out by a finite type quasicoherent sheaf of ideals I, then Bl_X Y = Proj_Y( O_Y ⊕ I ⊕ I^2 ⊕ I^3 ⊕ ··· ) (the Proj of the Rees algebra). This scheme satisfies the universal property of the blow-up, and the blow-up morphism is projective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 22.3.2. Because the graded algebra is generated in degree 1 and finite type hypotheses hold, Proj construction yields a projective morphism. This gives an explicit, globally-defined construction and proves existence in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional divisor described as a Proj over X
rubrics_metrics.description: EXY (the exceptional divisor) can be described as EXY = Proj_X( O_Y/I ⊕ I/I^2 ⊕ I^2/I^3 ⊕ ··· ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Displayed formula (22.3.2.1). Useful to think of the exceptional divisor as the projectivized normal cone and to compute its geometry; in good cases it is a projectivized normal bundle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal cone and tangent cone definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The normal cone N_{X}Y of X in Y is N_{X}Y := Spec_X( ⊕_{n≥0} I^n / I^{n+1} ). When X is a closed point p, this is the tangent cone at p; the projectivized tangent cone equals the exceptional divisor EXY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 22.3.6. This object is an algebraic 'infinitesimal tubular neighborhood'. Cautions: even if Y is smooth, N_{X}Y may fail to be smooth; even if both X and Y are smooth, N_{X}Y need not embed in Y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior for regular embeddings: identification with symmetric algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ Y is a regular embedding with ideal sheaf I generated locally by a regular sequence a1,...,ad, then the natural map Sym^n(I/I^2) → I^n / I^{n+1} is an isomorphism for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 22.3.8 (proof deferred). Consequences (22.3.D): the normal cone equals the total space of the normal sheaf (normal bundle), the exceptional divisor is the projectivized normal bundle, and the normal bundle to EXY in Bl_X Y restricts to O(−1) on projective fibers. Exercises and lemmas (22.3.E, 22.3.12) give proofs and algebraic details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal bundle to exceptional divisor in regular cases is O(−1)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the blow-up of a regular embedding, the exceptional divisor is a projective bundle over X and its normal bundle in the blow-up restricts to O(−1) on the projective fibers; in the plane-blow-up at a point the exceptional divisor has normal bundle O(−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 22.3.5 and Exercise 22.3.D(b). This is used in further results like Castelnuovo's Criterion for blowing-down (-1)-curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up preserves smoothness for smooth center and ambient
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ⊂ Y is a closed embedding of smooth varieties over a field k, then Bl_X Y is smooth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 22.3.10. Proof uses that EXY is a projective bundle (hence smooth) and that it is an effective Cartier divisor, so regularity/smoothness of Bl_X Y follows by slicing criterion. Use Exercise 22.3.D(a) and smoothness-regularity comparison (13.2.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit affine chart description for blow-up of A^2 at origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Bl_{(0,0)} A^2 = Proj k[x,y,X,Y] with relation xY − yX = 0; on the two standard P^1-patches [X:Y]=[s:1] and [1:t] one gets Spec k[x,y,s]/(sy − x) ≅ Spec k[y,s] and Spec k[x,y,t]/(y − xt) ≅ Spec k[x,t], both smooth. The exceptional divisor is principal on each patch (cut out by y on one patch and x on the other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 22.4.1. This gives practical computational coordinates for hand calculations; helps see that blow-up is smooth and what the exceptional divisor looks like locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach 1: explicit coordinate description (useful for calculations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When X is cut out by generators f1,...,fn in an affine A = Spec A, one can view Bl_X Y by pulling back from the universal blow-up Bl_{(x1,...,xn)} Spec Z[x1,...,xn] given by equations x_i X_j − x_j X_i = 0 in Spec Z[x1,...,xn] × P^{n−1}, and then taking the closure via the Blow-up Closure Lemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation in 22.3.4 and Approach 1; useful because it provides an explicit single-ring picture and is convenient for computations and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach 2: global Proj (conceptual and general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the blow-up uniformly as Proj_Y of the Rees algebra ⊕_{n≥0} I^n. This approach proves existence and projectivity and ties exceptional divisor and normal cone definitions into a single algebraic construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach 2 (Theorem 22.3.2) is conceptually cleaner and is used to prove the universal property; Approach 1 can be recovered as a special case and is often more computationally explicit.
